nameStory: The Indiana bat gets its name from the state where it was first scientifically described and studied. Indiana remains one of the key states in this endangered bat's limited range, though the species actually lives across much of the Midwest and Southeast. It's one of those animals whose common name ties it forever to the place where scientists first took notice!
description: The Indiana bat is a small, mouse-eared bat that's roughly the size of your thumb when folded up. These endangered bats weigh about as much as two pennies and have soft, fluffy fur that ranges from gray to chestnut brown. With their delicate pink lips and tiny dark eyes, they look almost mouse-like when seen up close. They're incredibly rare in New England, making any sighting a truly special event.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Tiny bat, only 1-2 inches long with a wingspan about the size of your hand spread wide. Body feels delicate and lightweight, weighing less than a quarter.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Soft, dense fur that feels almost velvety to the touch, colored gray, black, or warm chestnut brown. The fur has a slight sheen and lies smoothly against the body.

idTips.label: Feet & Toes
idTips.description: Notably small feet with short, sparse hair on the toes - much less fuzzy than the similar Little Brown Bat. The feet feel almost naked compared to other mouse-eared bats.

idTips.label: Face Features
idTips.description: Distinctive bright pink lips that stand out against the dark fur, and a small pink nose. The ears are medium-sized and darker than the face.

idTips.label: Wing Details
idTips.description: Wings have a small ridge or keel along the tail membrane near the foot - a technical feature called a 'keeled calcar' that experts use for identification.

habitat: In New England, Indiana bats would be found in mature hardwood forests, especially those with oak, hickory, and maple trees. They prefer areas near streams, rivers, or ponds where insects are abundant, often hunting over agricultural fields adjacent to forests. Given their extreme rarity here, any Indiana bat would likely be a vagrant far from their core Midwest range.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from hibernation in caves or mines, then disperses to summer roosts. Pregnant females would be seeking warm roost sites under loose bark of dead or dying trees.
seasonality.summer: Most active season, with mothers raising pups in small colonies. Hunt insects at dusk and dawn, often seen flying in steady, direct patterns about 10 feet above ground.
seasonality.fall: Begins migration back to hibernation sites, building up fat reserves for winter. May travel hundreds of miles to reach suitable caves or abandoned mines.
seasonality.winter: Deep hibernation in caves or mines with stable, cool temperatures. Clusters with other bats in tight groups to conserve body heat and energy.

funFact: Indiana bats are so loyal to their hibernation spots that they'll fly hundreds of miles to return to the exact same cave each winter - and amazingly, about 85% of the entire species hibernates in just a handful of caves across the Midwest!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from Little Brown Bats without handling - the key difference is Indiana bats have much less hair on their toes and smaller feet overall. Memory trick: 'Indiana bats have itty-bitty feet with barely any fuzz between the toes.'
contextualKnowledge: The Indiana bat is federally endangered with fewer than 500,000 individuals remaining. White-nose syndrome, a fungal disease that affects hibernating bats, has devastated populations. Any suspected Indiana bat sighting should be reported to wildlife authorities, as they're so rare in New England that documentation is crucial for conservation efforts.
compareHints: Among the mouse-eared bats, Indiana bats are most similar to Little Brown Bats but have smaller feet with less toe hair and distinctive pink lips. Northern Myotis have longer ears and different wing patterns, while Eastern Small-footed Myotis are noticeably smaller overall. The foot hair difference is the most reliable field mark when distinguishing from Little Brown Bats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the mouse-eared bats in New England, the little brown bat has the glossiest, most reflective fur compared to the Northern Myotis which appears more matte and grayish-brown.

Among New England's mouse-eared bats, the Northern Myotis stands out with its distinctively long ears - much longer than the Little Brown Bat's modest rounded ears or the Indiana Bat's medium-length ears.
Compared to its mouse-eared bat cousins like the Little Brown Bat and Northern Myotis, the Eastern Small-footed Myotis is noticeably smaller with that unmistakable black face mask.
